blocks.x: George Lewis, January 25, 1960, Reel 1. George Lewis, January 25, 1960.
George Lewis, January 25, 1960. Yeah, George's voice is the only one we really need to be good.

We'll ask him a question and he says yes and we won't be able to hear the question. Well, I was reminiscing last night about Manning's with you out there. Remember the first tune you always used to play is All I Do the Whole Day Through is Dream of You. What was that?
Well, I didn't notice, as you're in the time, Tawler was playing.
Yeah.
I think because he loved it better than anything else.
Really? It's all right. That was his favorite tune.

Yeah. I remember Bunk's band always used to start out at the same tune every night in New York, too. You always hurt the one you love. Always hurt the one you love. Is that because you all liked it or just something easy to get warmed up on? Something easy to get warmed up on.
That's about the whole thing about it.

One other thing before I forget, maybe interrupt the train of thought, but this idea of playing a piece twice quite often. Some dancers I used to go to here, they'd play almost every piece. They'd play it twice. As soon as they get through, if anybody applauds at all, they'd play it twice. Is that an old custom?

Well, that was an old custom because during the dance hall times, you know, when a ployer like that, well, you call it an end call. Yeah. But in the later years, it just won't win. You know, dances played out. There's no halls or anything to work in. And the old time, they just kept the...
Yeah. I like it. It's a nice idea. I mean, a piece is good, but I like to hear it two or three times. I just wondered, in the old days, they did that all the time then. That was done all the time.

Right on every tune, you know, that you played, if you got the applause, which you did during those days, you got a lot of applause. Excuse me. And then when Bunk went to New York, well, he had that habit, so he just kept it right going.
I know sometimes they play a piece two or sometimes three times. I think as many as four times. Did they do that in the old days, too? They played more than twice sometimes? Oh, yes.
Now, Kid Thomas still does that, but I noticed he never plays them more than about twice, huh?
Yeah. Sometimes three times. I remember in New York, sometimes they played them as many as four times. People would want to hear them, do they?

They'd want to hear them, and they were dancing, you see. Now there's no dancing going on, so it don't make much sense to play the same thing over. Probably you may play the same tune anyhow, three or four times a night. Yeah. Someone may come and ask to play a must-write rhyme with it, and the next set someone will come back and ask for the same thing. Before the set is over, someone will ask for the same thing.
Back to Manny's in those times, what tunes would you play for dancers especially there?

Well, we had a repertoire that we played like, we played a lot of the old poplin numbers, like the girl that you married was one. We used to play rumbles. We played practically everything. During those days.

Oh, that reminds me, the other day I got on the bus and John Casimir was there. So we're sitting down talking, he says, you're telling me down on Bourbon Street they never play a waltz. I can't understand that, you know? Yeah. Well, naturally, down there they don't want any waltzes.
No, they want everything loud, you know, to attract people's attention.
In the old days, did you, like you do over the waves when you play a waltz, did you play it then in foxtrot tempo after that, or, that is say, 40 years ago?
No, no, we never done the tempo. Just stick to the waltz? Just stick to the waltz, yeah. You might play medleys of waltzes, you know.
Or if you played the waltz twice then, did you ever play it the next time in regular dance tempo on foxtrot?
Never, never stepped it up, no.
Never did it, even on the second time that you played it. That's right.
We even played shawty's, we never, we played twice, sometimes three times.
Just the way it was written. Just the way it was written, yeah. Regular dance.
Talbot had a lot of good numbers. What were some of the numbers he had that are unusual? He don't play some of them anymore.
Well, it's kind of hard to get the men to play them. A lot of fellas don't really remember the numbers.
What about Red Rose Rag? Do you play that anymore?
No.
I think that's the name of it, huh? Or was it Rose Leaf?
Rose Leaf.
Rose Leaf Rag or Red Rose Rag?
No, Rose Leaf Rag.
Rose Leaf Rag, yeah, that was good.
Poirce's by the honest one plays a part of that. Howard, they don't play all of it.
Oh, another tune that they used to play, the Victory Waltz. I never could get that straight, what the tune is. If you can sort of hum it, or what was it? It wasn't really a waltz, was it? I heard it.
Well, a lot of people, you see, we people out here, our pronunciation is funny. A lot of people think we say Victory Waltz, but it's Victory Walk.
Oh, walk.
Yeah.
Oh, somebody else. The brass bands play that tune.
The brass bands play it. The Victory Walk. Victory Walk, yeah. How does it go?
Can you hear a little bit of it?
Uh, dun, Your record played it a lot.
Mm-hmm. A lot of people. Well, Joe Avery used to play that with a tuxedo a lot, too. Well, what is the name of that? Did that come out during the war, before, or what?
Uh, I'll tell you the truth, Rich, I really don't know where it came from. I know. Yeah. I played it, but I really couldn't say where it came from.
You don't remember how old it was, huh?
No. I knew I played it with a lot of brass bands. I played it with the Eureka. I even played it with, uh, Eddie Jackson's tuxedo.
Well, that must date back.
Well, it's dated way back, yeah. But, uh, how far back I really don't know.
How long has Eddie Jackson been dead?
Never did. No. Eddie Jackson's been dead, you know, close to 17, 18 years.
They buried him on April Fool's Day, I think.
Yeah, that's close to him.
I can't remember what year, though.
I never got to hear him. He was here, I guess, when I came down, but I never heard him.
Well, I wanted to tell you, you know who I see pretty often now is a little dad.
Oh, you do.
He's mighty sick. He can't even walk anymore. He's bedridden. Punch and I go by and see him. Can hardly hear, of course.

Well, he never could hear. Never could hear. I played with him a lot. During the time with, uh, Earl Humphrey, and Buddy Petit, and Eric Scott, that fellow. He always was hard of hearing, but he could hear the beat. Of course, he was a much younger man. He could hear the beat. But, uh, he couldn't tune his banjo.
He couldn't? Or he could?

He couldn't. I mean, just off the reel, you'd have to give him a note, a note for note. You know, like an ordinary banjo would get, uh, just the A, uh, the A string, you know, and go right on tune. He couldn't, but he couldn't hear it.
Mm-hmm. Oh. Anything else you want to ask about mayonnaise? Because I have some other things to ask.
Well, uh, yeah, I'm just trying to think of who you had out there. Let's see.
What do you mean? In the band.
It was a change in proposition. Before I got here, Moran was there.
Well, after Talbot died, we had Moran.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right. But I've been, even before that Moran was there, somebody told me. I don't know. I'll take it back. I'm not sure about that. That was before I got here, you know, and people tell you things. Yeah, I don't remember.
Yeah, I don't remember. Yeah, let's see.
After Talbot. When I first, I first went in there, I went in there just, uh, without a trumpet player at all. Yeah.
Mm-hmm. Well, I remember I came down here one New Year's Eve and you had no trombone.

Yeah, well, I never used a trombone out there until, uh, later years when the money wasn't very big, you know. Yeah. You couldn't afford to get out of a trombone player. So, people would get together, friends, and would, you know, make up Jim's salary. And that's how Jim would come in there. But, uh, hardly ever needed any extra men because always had a bunch of the young white boys would be out there. George Gerard and Pete Fonten and the Santo Brothers, they all really was out there. Bill Shea. Bill Shea. Yeah, right. Bob Nookie even stopped out there. A lot of guys.
Bob who?
Bob Nookie.
I can't remember him.
Mm. What did he play? Bob Nookie. Bob Nookie. Bob Nookie.
Bob Nookie. Bob Nookie, yeah.
Bob Nookie, yeah.
I'll see you around.
Mm.
Um, when was that big flood? The drags base got ruined and the guitar, everything.
Everything got ruined, uh, I think it was in the month of September. Big rainstorm.
About 49Storm.
About 49Storm. 47, was it? It was in 47. No, I think it was earlier than that.
46, maybe?
Around 46.
Just back from New York, right?
Yeah, around 46.
Well, let's see. I remember Tolka was in there a few nights, not long.
Yeah, he played in there.
And, of course, Percy was there for a while.
Excuse me.
When Ken came here, Percy was on trumpet, remember?
Yeah. Well, Talbot had him pass.
Yeah, Goodwild.
More and also there.

Well, that was when you were at the El Morocco. Your trumpet place kept dying on you. Yeah. 1951, that was about it. Those places will kill you. Percy came in then, and I guess you went back to Manny's after the El Morocco.
No, I didn't go back to Manny's. We'd spot around most of the time.
You were at Manny's in 1951. I'm pretty sure.
After a while you went back to Manny's, I'm sure, because when Ken was here, you were at Manny's. 1952.
That was when you were there. No, when Ken was here, I wasn't playing at Manny's. I waited a little place up there where they makes this.
Oh, Trios?
No, they makes this bread. This sunbeam bread up somewhere around the...
On Jefferson Davis?
Yeah.
Well, that's Trios Lounge. That's a... Remember Huey and Harry Marone had the record shop on Bourbon Street and they put up the money for the thing?
That's when Ken was here. I guess you were here.
Yeah, that was...
1952, 1953, that winter.
Yeah. And Percy was there sometimes.
Not 53. I don't know. I can stretch that. Yeah, we were out early part of 53.
Yeah, in that winter anyway.
Check with...

Late 53. Yeah. But, uh... Percy was there part of the time and Howard was there part of the time. Yeah. And lots of guys sat in out there, too. Yeah, I remember, because I was still, uh... I was going to say playing trombone. I better say I was studying trombone instead. I remember playing Tiger Rag with you.
Yeah.
You play with punch, Marge?

I played a couple of jobs with punch during the time when they... when they had the band with Eddie Morris and, uh... I worked in Georgia Boyd's place and... Uh... No, that was in the early... early...early 20th. But, uh... See, as a steady man, I never worked at, but... in fact, I played with practically every band in the Orleans, off and on, some... and so on,
And Ray Allen for a while, too, that's right.
Ray Allen? I played Ray Allen's father.
Did he have a dance band, or...
No, I had a brass band, yeah. Only brass band. A brass band, yeah.
Can you tell us a little bit more about Lee Collins when you played with him?

I played with Lee, yes. I played with Lee, with the, uh, Earl Humphrey's band. That's, uh, Lee joined the band right after Buddy Petit left. In fact, they fired Buddy Petit for Lee, on account of the drinking so much.
Um, did you remember you told about, you made some records once on Canal Street or someplace, with Lee, was that, what was that, can you remember any more details of that?
No, Bill, I can't remember.
Was it on Canal Street, or where was it?

It was on Canal Street, at the World Lines, I remember that as good. Yeah, it was on Canal Street, but, uh, I, I can't think of them no more about it, because probably we all were, well underneath the wind that day.
Yeah. Do you remember who was in the band about that time?

Well I know Lee was one and uh, drummer was uh, is he the Irvin Joseph? I think it was Irvin Joseph. A piano player by the name of Tink, we used to call him Tink, I never did know his other name. Baptiste. Baptiste something, I think he's been dead quite a while. He's been a hit.

I wonder if you could tell us some more about Isidore Fritz, since none of us ever met him or knew anything about the... Were there some other members of the family over there that played? All about Mandeville that you can remember when you were older.

Yeah, uh, it was, Isidore was a clarinetist, his father was a bass player, and his brother was a trombone player, and uh, uh, Claybear Canginella, uh, Orny, you know Orny, his brother was a drummer, and at one time Bunk was a trumpet player. Bunk was a trumpet player. Well, his daughter was about the best man I ever heard. I mean, if a man played on a order like I played, never read a note in his life.
Never heard, he's the best you ever heard in your whole life, you mean any place, huh?

Any place. Any place. And uh, they had a real, real good band. And there was uh, Leonard Parker around there, there was Tommy Ladner. Leonard Parker was out of Slide Hill, I played with him quite a while. And then Dan Moody, during that time Dan was playing uh, trombone instead of, and he got off the trombone and went, got back on the bass violin.
Who was that foul singer over there, Black Eagle?
Oh, Black Eagle, well he's still, I think someone told me he's still around there yet. He was pretty good, that's a little band I played with over there.
You say he's in Mandeville? He's in Mandeville now, yes.
I don't find him. Uh, Andrew Anderson told me he saw him just recently. Andrew Anderson, he come from the same place too. He don't play anymore.
You know who's over there too, is Wilhelmina Ball. He says Wilhelmina Ball is over there in Lacombe. We'll have to take a trip over there Bill.
Uh huh. Uh, what did those bands play for? Mostly dances or parties or on a boat or anything?

Well they played, they played uh, dances and they done a lot of uh, local traveling. Around from country to country like uh, all the way into Electric Mill, Mississippi, or around Lumberton, Meridian, uh, Jackson, Mississippi, all around in that neighborhood. We played in different places. We'd meet the boat, the idle hour, and also the Hanover and the Susquehanna, those riverboats, that was right after the Camilla. We'd stop running, we'd meet them at the pier, you know. They come across the lake? They come across the lake from uh, from uh, uh, Was it West End or Spanish Fork? No they came from Millenbury. Millenbury. From Millenbury, yes. Millenbury.
Um, did they have any brass bands over there that you can remember?
No they didn't have any brass bands over there in that time, no. No brass bands.
Did your bands uh, that you played with, or the Fritz uh, band, any of those come over here to play dances that you know?
No, not, not that I know of. It was, uh, that's the cause of me to come over here to play, see I lived at this Manable during that time.
But did you live there all the time or just for the summers?

No, you see, my family and I, we were minding a club, and regalese, and I was a club, and regalese, you know? And uh, my oldest daughter, Mildred, she was a small child, she was taken with terrible fever from mosquito bites, and the doctor ordered me to take her, thought probably she had some lung trouble or something, to bring her over there in his party. But my father was over in that neighborhood, so I just brought her. Well I joined the Black Eagles band, and I played with Leonard Parker, and uh, uh, Fritz played a while with Buddy Petit and he gave it up, quit the band because he was in the business of a brick, brick mason. So I joined Buddy Petit's band, not either, Edmund Hall got in the Buddy Petit's band, and I stayed with Leonard Parker. So when uh, Edmund Hall left him, and they wanted to bring uh, Isidore Fritz over, he wouldn't leave him, he never did want to come to the New Orleans. Who was it, was it the Brick Mason? Isidore Fritz. They were brick, yeah they were all bricklayers. Bricklayers. Yeah, that was my trade. And so I came on over with uh, well I'd come over week, every week, around Wednesday, and I'd stay with my mother and go back on Monday or whatever date, you know, the job would be over with. And then I just decided to move back here, but all the way they lived right here would cause me to go to that neighborhood instead of coming back to New Orleans on account of uh, Mirit being sick, yeah.
When you came back over here, you worked with Billy and the Dee some, didn't you?

Yeah, I worked with Billy and the Dee, I worked with uh, George, George Anderson, I worked with uh, Wooden Joe, when Wooden Joe had a real old Wooden Joe's band with uh, with uh, Johnny Proudos, Buddy Luck, John Smith, uh, Edmund Garman, uh.
What did Buddy Luck play?
He was a bass player. And what was Gohmann playing then?
The saxophone, playing on the saxophone.

And uh, Ambrose, an uncle to uh, Lawrence Tucker, played the trombone. Then I waited a while with uh, Amos Riley, up in uh, up there in uh, 12th Ward. And I waited with uh, Ted O'Harris. Well a lot of the, the old had been gone a long time.
You said O'Harris, I didn't play the trumpet player.
He's been on a lot of, all of them been gone.
That's not Kid O'Harris. No, no.
He's uh, this guy was a big, heavy set guy, larger than Bill, but uh, he was a trumpet player. He was running a cleaning, cleaning, uh, business.
Uh, why did you work with Billy and Dede?

Well during the, I started working with them during the Depression. Right there at Decatur and Ursuline, the Kingfish. That's where I worked with them. I worked there, and over two years, about two and a half years, close, for a dollar a night there. From eight to three in the morning.
Fantastic. Who was in the band then?

There was only four of us in there. It was Billy, when we first started it was Burtz. Burtz Stevenson was playing trumpet. It was Burtz, myself, Billy, and uh, a fella by the name of McGee, playing drum. Dede, he was working further down on Decatur Street, between St. Philip and uh, Dumaine, right close to where there's Vincent. The Lucas have the hardware. And then they, they fell in love with one another. And they got married. I was, I was the best man for their wedding. And that's where Billy got, uh, boys fired and brought Dede in there. And then, uh, we got different drummers after that. Uh, Smilin' Joe, they increased the band. Smilin' Joe, he came in there playing a five string, a four string guitar, ukulele style. And then the tambourines had flow shows and everything. And the first place where we, uh, run into major bowls. Where they wanted to take us off. We, we kind of, you know, think we're bad hair, we wouldn't take any chances of going any place.
He came by and heard you there? Yes.
They used to have a lot of celebrities on the gay street. That seems strange now. They had nothing but winos.

It was wild then, I'm telling you. Had wine on them and everything? Yeah, it was pretty wild. Yeah, I worked there for two years and a half almost. It was one dollar a night. Some nights I would go home with a dollar, some nights I would go home with a dollar and a quarter, some nights I would go home with a little more, some nights just that dollar. I never miss a night in two years and a half. That's how I got that metal clarinet.
How many nights a week? Seven nights a week.
Seven nights a week.
Seven?
Did you get tips sometimes or playing songs or people? Well, we were allowed to pass a kitty. Oh. But it was mostly local people, you know, and we didn't think of very much.
Did you have any other job? Did you do any of the work on the record?

During that time, I was working for the PWA. I had to get up at six o'clock in the morning and catch the bus and work until two in the evening. And then I'd come home and sleep and I'd meet this job. I started at the riverfront around 37.

Did you work mostly in the coffee? I remember once you were in New York, you demonstrated how they used to boost the coffee. One fellow was called the booster. Yeah. Did you lift those coffee sacks up? Yeah. Sorry, but a little one.
Mostly coffee I worked in. Sometime I'd truck the cotton, but it was mostly coffee.
When they'd lift, though, they'd have four people, was it one on each corner? No, three.
Three? Three, yeah. And one fellow? One to boost. Yeah, it all depends for the height, you know. Yeah. One would boost, yeah.
I can't get that picture in my mind. How does that work?
You see one man on each end of the bag, and the other man, when the two rays, the other man gets underneath, pushes, you see, and makes the bag flip over.
Did you sing any work songs in those days?
No, I never was a singer.
Did you hear any, though?

Well, those fellows didn't do much singing out on the riverfront, though. Not on the riverfront? No, the riverfront, I tell you, the riverfront always was a tough, tough job. And every man that worked it out there was what they call ornery. He was mean. I mean, during his working time he was absolutely mean to his own stuff, because the work was hard.
I thought you told me in New York that they had sort of, they counted it out some way, so they'd have a rhythm to boosting that up there to the right time.

Yeah, well, you see, they would have a rhythm to say, like you'd say, one, two, hup, one, two, hup, you know, this, on the third one, that one man would pick up before the other one would hurt one another.
You showed me where you hurt your wrist there once you, when you did it too soon. Yeah, it comes out yet.
Still got a bump on there. Yeah, it comes out. It was out last week, it was like that, I suffered there.
Really? Yeah. Still, you didn't hit it in time, or too soon or something?
Too soon, you hit it too soon, or it wouldn't pick up right, you could hurt yourself. Yeah.
How much did you weigh then?

I weighed around about 121. And how much did you weigh? Then I started losing weight. After I got operated on the, I was already in the stomach, I started losing, and I got onto 114 and I stayed there, I continued working, and then all the days I started, blood counts got bad, and I don't know, I was hot and everything started getting well, I went down, now I weighed about 104.
How much does the coffee sacks weigh?
How much did you weigh? 136 pounds.
More than you huh? Mm-mm. Oh, you ever work at Lutton's? Oh yeah. Sure. I worked at Lutton's, I worked there with Bill and the D and M too. I worked there a long while.

I put Big Guy Louie there. I put Rogers, Ernest Rogers there. I worked there a long while. I worked there a long while. I worked with them at the Silver Store at St. Claude and St. Bernard. St. But there stuff I worked there a long while. I worked with them at the Silver Star at St. Claude and St. Bernard. I worked there with them a long while. But they were terrible people. They were terrible.
You told me once how much he could drink on a job. How many cases of beer could he drink?
He drank two or three cases of beer a night. That's a fact. That's the truth. I'm not joking. I'm not going to tell you where to lie. She would drink.
At night, I worked with them in Bunky, and they would, we'd soon walk in and the man would pay it off. And he'd order two case of beer, and she'd order a gallon of sherry wine.
Who was up there in Bunky?
Myself, and it was a very good tramo player, I can't call his name now, but I know he's
a dude.
Frankie Gibbs. Frankie Gibbs. He was a cripple.
Were you around when Dee Dee made up Beyba Ba?
Well, I was around, yes I was around. It had been many years ago, I can't tell you what year it was.
Do you remember anything about the circumstances?
No, I really don't know because so many people claim it, but from the older people I hear, it's been around before Dee Dee's time.
Oh yes, I know one version of it, but the jazz form of it is his, isn't it?
Well as much as I know, the rest of it I know, it really is, yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Who else was in Bunky now?
There was Joe Phillips on the banjo, that's the one I'd be sung.
Yeah.
And Gibbs, myself, Billy Dee Dee. Someone else, I'm trying to think.
Saxophone?
No, we didn't have any saxophone.
There's the end of that. That's all. stuff

segments.title: Opening tunes and repeating pieces for dancers at Manny's
segments.summary: Allen and Russell ask about the first tune played at Manny's, and about the old custom of playing a piece twice or more when dancers applauded. Lewis says it faded once dancing stopped.

segments.title: Dance repertoire at Manny's: waltzes and old numbers
segments.summary: Lewis lists the old popular numbers and waltzes the band played for dancers, never speeding the waltz into foxtrot tempo. Bourbon Street bands no longer play waltzes.

segments.title: Rose Leaf Rag and the Victory Walk brass band tune
segments.summary: They sort out the title Rose Leaf Rag and the brass band tune Victory Walk, which Lewis played with the Eureka and Eddie Jackson's Tuxedo band. Lewis does not know its origin.

segments.title: Little Dad, ill and hard of hearing
segments.summary: Allen reports that Little Dad is bedridden. Lewis recalls playing with him in the Humphrey and Buddy Petit bands; he could hear the beat but could not tune his banjo.

segments.title: Who played in the Manny's band: Talbert, Morand, no trombone, young white sitters-in
segments.summary: Lewis recalls Moran coming in after Talbot died and seldom using a trombone because money was short. Young white players such as George Girard, Pete Fountain and the Assunto brothers often sat in.

segments.title: The flood that ruined the instruments
segments.summary: They try to date the storm that ruined the drums and guitar, settling on around 1946, just after Lewis's return from New York.

segments.title: Trumpeters and venues around Ken Colyer's visit, 1951-53
segments.summary: Allen and Lewis reconstruct who played trumpet at Manny's, the El Morocco and the bread-company lounge while Ken was in New Orleans, with Percy and Howard sitting in.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Fritz family in Mandeville
segments.title: Lewis on playing with many bands, Punch Miller and Ray Allen's father
segments.summary: Lewis says he played a few jobs with Punch and worked in Georgia Boyd's place, and played with nearly every New Orleans band off and on, including a brass band led by Allen's father.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Fritz family in Mandeville
segments.title: Lee Collins in the Humphrey band and a Canal Street record date
segments.summary: Lewis recalls Lee Collins replacing Buddy Petit, fired for drinking, in Earl Humphrey's band. He half-remembers a record session on Canal Street and its band members.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Fritz family in Mandeville
segments.title: The Fritz family band and musicians of Mandeville
segments.summary: Lewis describes Isidore Fritz, his family of musicians, and others in the Mandeville bands such as Leonard Parker and Black Eagle. Allen and Russell talk of tracking down surviving players.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Fritz family in Mandeville
segments.title: What the Mandeville bands played for and where they travelled
segments.summary: Lewis says the bands played dances and travelled to Mississippi towns and lake steamers. There were no brass bands there, and the bands did not come to New Orleans.

segments.chapter: Early bands and the Fritz family in Mandeville
segments.title: Why Lewis lived in Mandeville and moved back to New Orleans
segments.summary: His daughter's fever sent him to the north shore, where he joined Black Eagle's band and Leonard Parker's. He commuted weekly to New Orleans before moving back.

segments.chapter: Billy and De De Pierce at the Kingfish
segments.title: Bands Lewis worked with back in New Orleans
segments.summary: After returning, Lewis worked with Billy and De De Pierce, George Anderson, Wooden Joe and others, with Allen asking about their sidemen.

segments.chapter: Billy and De De Pierce at the Kingfish
segments.title: The Kingfish job with Billy and De De at a dollar a night
segments.summary: During the Depression Lewis worked seven nights a week at Decatur and Ursuline for about a dollar a night. He describes the band, Billy and De De marrying, and the rough crowd.

segments.chapter: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
segments.title: Riverfront work: PWA job, coffee sacks and boosting
segments.summary: Alongside music, Lewis worked on the riverfront from about 1937, mostly with coffee. He explains the three-man boosting method, the counting rhythm, and the wrist injury from lifting too soon.

segments.chapter: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
segments.title: Lewis's weight and health
segments.summary: Lewis gives his weight around 121 pounds, and how it fell after an operation and low blood counts. They compare it with the weight of a coffee sack.

segments.chapter: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
segments.title: Playing at Lutton's and the Silver Star with Billy and De De
segments.summary: Lewis recalls long stretches at Lutton's and the Silver Star, where the owners drank heavily. Another job with Frankie Gibbs is mentioned.

segments.chapter: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
segments.title: De De Pierce and the origin of Eh La Bas
segments.summary: Lewis was around when De De made up the tune, but cannot date it. Older people say it predates De De, though the jazz version is his.

segments.chapter: Day jobs and later Billy and De De engagements
segments.title: Personnel of the band, and end of reel
segments.summary: Lewis names the band members, banjo player Joe Phillips, Gibbs, himself and Billy and De De. The tape ends.
